Tor and Ext vanishing results for commutative Artinian rings

Bernhard Böhmler B. BöhmlerLeibniz Universität Hannover, Institut für Algebra, Zahlentheorie und Diskrete Mathematik, Welfengarten 1, 30167 Hannover, Germany Email address: boehmler@math.uni-hannover.de and René Marczinzik R. MarczinzikMathematical Institute of the University of Bonn, Endenicher Allee 60, 53115 Bonn, Germany Email address: marczire@math.uni-bonn.de
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We give a negative answer to a question of Avramov, Buchweitz and Şega by constructing a commutative local finite-dimensional non-Gorenstein algebra RR with ExtR1⁡(D⁡(R),R)=0\operatorname{Ext}_{R}^{1}(D(R),R)=0; this question is related to the first Tachikawa conjecture. We also give a counterexample to a conjecture of Huneke, Şega and Vraciu on Tor vanishing over commutative finite-dimensional algebras. Finally, we construct a finite-dimensional commutative local self-injective algebra RR over 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2} and an indecomposable non-projective RR-module MM such that ExtR1⁡(M,M)=ExtR2⁡(M,M)=0\operatorname{Ext}_{R}^{1}(M,M)=\operatorname{Ext}_{R}^{2}(M,M)=0, related to the second Tachikawa conjecture and answering a question of Dao.

Key words and phrases: 
Tachikawa conjectures, Tor vanishing, Ext vanishing, Gorenstein rings
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 13D07, 13E10

Introduction

In the book [Ta], Tachikawa formulated two homological conjectures for finite-dimensional, not necessarily commutative, KK-algebras (KK a field) that are closely related to the famous Nakayama conjecture. The Tachikawa conjectures remain open in general and are known only in special situations. They follow from the celebrated finitistic dimension conjecture; see, for example, the survey [Y]. The first Tachikawa conjecture states that, for a finite-dimensional KK-algebra AA with dual D⁡(A)=HomK⁡(A,K)D(A)=\operatorname{Hom}_{K}(A,K), the vanishing ExtAi⁡(D⁡(A),A)=0\operatorname{Ext}_{A}^{i}(D(A),A)=0 for all i≥1i\geq 1 implies that AA is self-injective. The second Tachikawa conjecture states that, if AA is self-injective and MM is an indecomposable AA-module satisfying ExtAi⁡(M,M)=0\operatorname{Ext}_{A}^{i}(M,M)=0 for all i≥1i\geq 1, then MM is projective. Both conjectures remain open even for finite-dimensional commutative algebras, but several commutative cases are known. For a proof of the conjectures over commutative local Artinian algebras with radical cube zero, see Asashiba and Hoshino [A, H, H2]. For broader background on the noncommutative conjectures, see [CFX, Sa].

In positive Krull dimension, the natural commutative analogue of the first conjecture replaces the vector-space dual by a canonical module in the Cohen–Macaulay case, or more generally by a dualizing complex. Avramov, Buchweitz and Şega formulated this version and proved it in several classes of commutative Noetherian local rings [ABS]. Further work treats Cohen–Macaulay tensor products [Jor], generically Gorenstein Cohen–Macaulay rings [GT], and positively graded rings over fields of characteristic different from two [LMSW]. Related Ext-vanishing criteria for the Gorenstein property were obtained by Hanes and Huneke [HH]; Lyle and Montaño later established further criteria based on consecutive blocks of Ext vanishing [LM]. A nearly Gorenstein variant, formulated via the trace of the canonical module, was posed by Dao, Kobayashi and Takahashi [DKT]; more recent annihilator-theoretic generalizations and results in Krull dimensions one, two and higher appear in [Es].

The resulting dualizing-complex conjecture is the following:

Conjecture.

Let RR be a commutative Noetherian local ring with dualizing complex DRD^{R}. If ExtRi⁡(DR,R)=0\operatorname{Ext}_{R}^{i}(D^{R},R)=0 for all i≥1i\geq 1, then RR is Gorenstein.

We refer to the introduction of [ABS] for this conjecture and the precise definition of DRD^{R}. In the introduction of [ABS], one can find the following question:

Question.

Let RR be a commutative Noetherian local ring with dualizing complex DRD^{R}. If ExtRi⁡(DR,R)=0\operatorname{Ext}_{R}^{i}(D^{R},R)=0 for dimR+1\dim R+1 consecutive positive values of ii, must RR be Gorenstein?

Note that, when RR is a commutative local finite-dimensional KK-algebra, it is Cohen–Macaulay and DR=HomK⁡(R,K)=D⁡(R)D^{R}=\operatorname{Hom}_{K}(R,K)=D(R). We give a negative answer as follows:

Theorem 0.1.

There exists a finite-dimensional commutative local non-Gorenstein ℚ\mathbb{Q}-algebra RR such that ExtR1⁡(D⁡(R),R)=0\operatorname{Ext}_{R}^{1}(D(R),R)=0.

This example was found with the assistance of ChatGPT and is rather complicated: it has 18 generators and many relations. We give its explicit presentation in Section 2, together with Magma code verifying the theorem.

Next we consider the second Tachikawa conjecture for commutative local finite-dimensional Gorenstein algebras. For commutative Artinian local rings, being Gorenstein is equivalent to being self-injective. In [D, Question 9.1.4], Dao posed the following question:

Question.

Let RR be a commutative local finite-dimensional Gorenstein algebra with a finitely generated module MM. If ExtR1⁡(M,M)=0\operatorname{Ext}_{R}^{1}(M,M)=0, is MM free?

Note that over local finite dimensional algebras, being free is equivalent to being projective for finitely generated modules. For commutative Artinian Gorenstein rings, the second Tachikawa conjecture is equivalent to the commutative Auslander–Reiten conjecture, which is discussed for example, in [S]. In positive Krull dimension, the latter asks whether a finitely generated module MM over a commutative Noetherian local ring RR satisfying

ExtRi⁡(M,M⊕R)=0for all ​i≥1\operatorname{Ext}_{R}^{i}(M,M\oplus R)=0\qquad\text{for all }i\geq 1

must be free. Auslander, Ding and Solberg proved the conjecture for complete intersections [ADS], and Huneke and Leuschke proved it for locally excellent Cohen–Macaulay normal rings containing the rational numbers [HL]. It was subsequently established for Cohen–Macaulay normal rings by Kimura, Otake and Takahashi [KOT], and more recently for every normal ring by Kimura [Ki]. Results for Gorenstein rings and extensions to Cohen–Macaulay local rings with canonical modules appear in [Ar, OY, ACST]; the rank-one maximal Cohen–Macaulay case is treated in [GT]. Further numerical cases and generalizations based on Ext annihilators are developed in [LM, Es].

Our next main result gives a negative answer to Dao’s question:

Theorem 0.2.

There is a finite-dimensional commutative local Gorenstein 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2}-algebra RR admitting an indecomposable non-projective RR-module MM such that ExtRi⁡(M,M)=0\operatorname{Ext}_{R}^{i}(M,M)=0 for i=1,2i=1,2.

We display the concrete algebra RR and module MM, which were also found with the assistance of ChatGPT, in Section 3, together with Magma code verifying the theorem. This also resolves a problem in the literature that had remained open for nearly 20 years. In [LH, Theorem 4.6] a result was presented that would imply that if RR is a commutative local finite-dimensional Gorenstein algebra and MM is an indecomposable RR-module satisfying ExtRi⁡(M,M)=0\operatorname{Ext}_{R}^{i}(M,M)=0 for i=1,2i=1,2, then MM is projective. This would imply the second Tachikawa conjecture in the commutative case. Doubts about the argument have been expressed for a long time, but no concrete counterexample was previously known; see, for example, the footnote on the first page of [S]. The theorem above supplies such a counterexample and shows that the argument in [LH, Theorem 4.6] cannot be correct. We remark that our previous two theorems also answer questions raised in [MO, Questions 2.4 and 2.5].

The last homological problem that we look at in this article is the following conjecture by Huneke, Şega and Vraciu in [HSV]:

Conjecture.

Let RR be a commutative Artinian local ring with maximal ideal 𝔪\mathfrak{m}. Assume that there are two nonzero finitely generated RR-modules MM and NN with 𝔪2​M=0\mathfrak{m}^{2}M=0 and 𝔪2​N=0\mathfrak{m}^{2}N=0. If ToriR⁡(M,N)=0\operatorname{Tor}_{i}^{R}(M,N)=0 for all i≥1i\geq 1, then 𝔪3=0\mathfrak{m}^{3}=0.

The next theorem gives a counterexample to this conjecture:

Theorem 0.3.

Let KK be a field, let R=K⁡[x,y]/(x​y,x2−y3)R=K[x,y]/(xy,x^{2}-y^{3}), set 𝔪=(x,y)​R\mathfrak{m}=(x,y)R, and let M=R/(y)M=R/(y) and N=R/(x−y)N=R/(x-y). Then 𝔪2​M=0\mathfrak{m}^{2}M=0, 𝔪2​N=0\mathfrak{m}^{2}N=0, and ToriR⁡(M,N)=0\operatorname{Tor}_{i}^{R}(M,N)=0 for all i≥1i\geq 1, whereas 𝔪3≠0\mathfrak{m}^{3}\neq 0.

The algebra RR was also found with the assistance of ChatGPT. The algebra RR is five-dimensional, and in this case we give a direct verification in Section 1.

For the computer verifications, the reader may copy and paste the relevant code into the Magma online calculator if the commercial version of Magma is unavailable: https://magma.maths.usyd.edu.au/calc/. We assume the reader is familiar with commutative algebra and refer for example to the textbook [E].

1. A counterexample to the conjecture of Huneke, Şega and Vraciu

In this section we prove the following theorem:

Theorem 1.1.

Let KK be a field and set

R=K⁡[x,y]/(x​y,x2−y3),M=R/(y),N=R/(x−y).R=K[x,y]/(xy,x^{2}-y^{3}),\qquad M=R/(y),\qquad N=R/(x-y).

Let 𝔪=(x,y)​R\mathfrak{m}=(x,y)R be the maximal ideal of RR. Then

𝔪2​M=0,𝔪2​N=0,ToriR⁡(M,N)=0for every ​i≥1,\mathfrak{m}^{2}M=0,\qquad\mathfrak{m}^{2}N=0,\qquad\operatorname{Tor}_{i}^{R}(M,N)=0\quad\text{for every }i\geq 1,

whereas 𝔪3≠0\mathfrak{m}^{3}\neq 0.

Proof.

Put

P=K⁡[X,Y],I=(X​Y,X2−Y3)⊆P,P=K[X,Y],\qquad I=(XY,X^{2}-Y^{3})\subseteq P,

and let

R=P/I.R=P/I.

We denote the residue classes of XX and YY in RR by xx and yy, respectively. Thus the defining relations in RR are

(1.1) x​y=0,x2=y3.xy=0,\qquad x^{2}=y^{3}.

We shall verify all assertions in the theorem directly.

Step 1: the vector-space structure of RR, its maximal ideal, and its Loewy length.

We first determine a KK-basis of RR. Consider the intermediate quotient

S=P/(X2−Y3),S=P/(X^{2}-Y^{3}),

and write x~\widetilde{x} and y~\widetilde{y} for the images of XX and YY in SS. Regard P=K​[Y]​[X]P=K[Y][X] as a polynomial ring in the one variable XX with coefficients in K⁡[Y]K[Y]. The polynomial X2−Y3X^{2}-Y^{3} is monic as a polynomial in XX. Hence the ordinary one-variable division algorithm shows that every polynomial p∈Pp\in P can be written uniquely in the form

Consequently, every element of SS has a unique expression

(1.2) f⁡(y~)+x~​g​(y~),f,g∈K⁡[Y].f(\widetilde{y})+\widetilde{x}g(\widetilde{y}),\qquad f,g\in K[Y].

The ring RR is obtained from SS by imposing the additional relation x~​y~=0\widetilde{x}\widetilde{y}=0. We now describe the ideal generated by x~​y~\widetilde{x}\widetilde{y} in SS. Using the unique expression in (1.2), an arbitrary multiple of x~​y~\widetilde{x}\widetilde{y} has the form

(f⁡(y~)+x~​g​(y~))​x~​y~\displaystyle\bigl(f(\widetilde{y})+\widetilde{x}g(\widetilde{y})\bigr)\widetilde{x}\widetilde{y} =x~​y~​f​(y~)+x~2​y~​g​(y~)\displaystyle=\widetilde{x}\widetilde{y}f(\widetilde{y})+\widetilde{x}^{2}\widetilde{y}g(\widetilde{y})
=x~​y~​f​(y~)+y~4​g​(y~),\displaystyle=\widetilde{x}\widetilde{y}f(\widetilde{y})+\widetilde{y}^{4}g(\widetilde{y}),

because x~2=y~3\widetilde{x}^{2}=\widetilde{y}^{3} in SS. Conversely, every sum of a multiple of y~4\widetilde{y}^{4} and a multiple of x~​y~\widetilde{x}\widetilde{y} occurs in this way. The uniqueness in (1.2) also shows that the two types of summands cannot cancel each other. Thus, as a KK-vector space,

(x~​y~)​S=y~4​K​[y~]⊕x~​y~​K​[y~].(\widetilde{x}\widetilde{y})S=\widetilde{y}^{4}K[\widetilde{y}]\mathbin{\oplus}\widetilde{x}\widetilde{y}K[\widetilde{y}].

It follows that every element of R=S/(x~​y~)R=S/(\widetilde{x}\widetilde{y}) has a unique representative of the form

a+b​x+c​y+d​y2+e​y3,a,b,c,d,e∈K.a+bx+cy+dy^{2}+ey^{3},\qquad a,b,c,d,e\in K.

Therefore

(1.3) 1,x,y,y2,y31,\quad x,\quad y,\quad y^{2},\quad y^{3}

is a KK-basis of RR. In particular,

dimKR=5andy3≠0.\dim_{K}R=5\qquad\text{and}\qquad y^{3}\neq 0.

We next record some immediate consequences of the defining relations. Multiplying x2=y3x^{2}=y^{3} by yy gives

x2​y=y4.x^{2}y=y^{4}.

The left-hand side is x⁡(x​y)=0x(xy)=0. Hence

(1.4) y4=0.y^{4}=0.

Also,

x3=x⋅x2=x​y3=y2​(x​y)=0.x^{3}=x\cdot x^{2}=xy^{3}=y^{2}(xy)=0.

Let

𝔪=(x,y)​R.\mathfrak{m}=(x,y)R.

By the basis in (1.3), the ideal 𝔪\mathfrak{m} is the KK-vector space

(1.5) 𝔪=K​x⊕K​y⊕K​y2⊕K​y3.\mathfrak{m}=Kx\oplus Ky\oplus Ky^{2}\oplus Ky^{3}.

The ideal 𝔪2\mathfrak{m}^{2} is generated by the pairwise products of xx and yy. Therefore, using (1.1),

𝔪2=(x2,x​y,y2)=(y3,0,y2)=(y2,y3).\mathfrak{m}^{2}=(x^{2},xy,y^{2})=(y^{3},0,y^{2})=(y^{2},y^{3}).

We now identify this ideal as a vector space. If r=a+b​x+c​y+d​y2+e​y3r=a+bx+cy+dy^{2}+ey^{3}, then

r​y2=a​y2+c​y3andr​y3=a​y3,ry^{2}=ay^{2}+cy^{3}\qquad\text{and}\qquad ry^{3}=ay^{3},

because x​y=0xy=0 and y4=0y^{4}=0. Thus

(1.6) 𝔪2=K​y2⊕K​y3.\mathfrak{m}^{2}=Ky^{2}\oplus Ky^{3}.

Multiplying once more by 𝔪\mathfrak{m}, we use

x​y2=x​y3=0,y⋅y2=y3,y⋅y3=y4=0,xy^{2}=xy^{3}=0,\qquad y\cdot y^{2}=y^{3},\qquad y\cdot y^{3}=y^{4}=0,

𝔪4=𝔪​𝔪3=0,\mathfrak{m}^{4}=\mathfrak{m}\mathfrak{m}^{3}=0,

because both x​y3xy^{3} and y4y^{4} are zero. Thus 𝔪\mathfrak{m} has nilpotency index four.

Since dimKR=5\dim_{K}R=5, the ring RR is Artinian. To prove that it is local, evaluate at X=Y=0X=Y=0. This induces a surjective ring homomorphism

π:R⟶K,π⁡(a+b​x+c​y+d​y2+e​y3)=a.\pi:R\longrightarrow K,\qquad\pi(a+bx+cy+dy^{2}+ey^{3})=a.

Step 2: the modules MM and NN, and the action of 𝔪2\mathfrak{m}^{2}.

The modules M=R/(y)M=R/(y) and N=R/(x−y)N=R/(x-y) are cyclic quotient modules, so they are finitely generated. They are also quotients of RR by an ideal and thus KK-algebras. We now describe them explicitly via their KK-algebra and RR-module structure and in particular show that they are 2-dimensional as a vector space over KK. As they have simple top, they are indecomposable.

In M=R/(y)M=R/(y), the element yy acts as zero, and the relation x2=y3x^{2}=y^{3} therefore becomes x2=0x^{2}=0. The assignment

t⟼x+(y)t\longmapsto x+(y)

defines a surjective KK-algebra homomorphism

K⁡[t]/(t2)⟶M.K[t]/(t^{2})\longrightarrow M.

Conversely, the assignments x↦tx\mapsto t and y↦0y\mapsto 0 define a homomorphism R→K⁡[t]/(t2)R\to K[t]/(t^{2}): indeed, both x​yxy and x2−y3x^{2}-y^{3} are sent to zero. This homomorphism kills the ideal (y)(y), so it factors through MM. The two induced maps are inverse to one another because they agree with the identity on the generators. Consequently,

(1.8) M≅K⁡[t]/(t2).M\cong K[t]/(t^{2}).

In particular, MM is nonzero and has KK-basis 1,t1,t.

For N=R/(x−y)N=R/(x-y), let

u=x+(x−y)=y+(x−y)u=x+(x-y)=y+(x-y)

be the common image of xx and yy. The relation x​y=0xy=0 gives u2=0u^{2}=0. Therefore the assignment u↦x+(x−y)u\mapsto x+(x-y) gives a surjective homomorphism

K⁡[u]/(u2)⟶N.K[u]/(u^{2})\longrightarrow N.

Conversely, sending both xx and yy to uu defines a homomorphism R→K⁡[u]/(u2)R\to K[u]/(u^{2}), because

x​y⟼u2=0andx2−y3⟼u2−u3=0.xy\longmapsto u^{2}=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad x^{2}-y^{3}\longmapsto u^{2}-u^{3}=0.

It also sends x−yx-y to zero, so it factors through NN. Again the two induced maps are inverse on the generators. Hence

(1.9) N≅K⁡[u]/(u2).N\cong K[u]/(u^{2}).

Thus NN is nonzero and has KK-basis 1,u1,u.

By (1.6), the ideal 𝔪2\mathfrak{m}^{2} is spanned by y2y^{2} and y3y^{3}. On MM, the element yy acts as zero, so both y2y^{2} and y3y^{3} act as zero. On NN, the element yy acts as uu, and u2=0u^{2}=0, so again both y2y^{2} and y3y^{3} act as zero. Therefore

(1.10) 𝔪2​M=0and𝔪2​N=0.\mathfrak{m}^{2}M=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathfrak{m}^{2}N=0.

Moreover, 𝔪​M≠0\mathfrak{m}M\neq 0 because x⋅1=t≠0x\cdot 1=t\neq 0 in MM, and 𝔪​N≠0\mathfrak{m}N\neq 0 because x⋅1=u≠0x\cdot 1=u\neq 0 in NN. Thus both modules have Loewy length exactly two.

Every element r∈Rr\in R has a unique expression

Step 4: an explicit two-periodic free resolution of MM.

Let Fi=RF_{i}=R for every i≥0i\geq 0, and let

ε:F0=R⟶M=R/(y)\varepsilon:F_{0}=R\longrightarrow M=R/(y)

be the quotient map. For i≥1i\geq 1, define an RR-linear map di:Fi→Fi−1d_{i}:F_{i}\to F_{i-1} by

di​(r)={r​y,if i is odd,r​x,if i is even.d_{i}(r)=\begin{cases}ry,&\text{if $i$ is odd},\\ rx,&\text{if $i$ is even}.\end{cases}

(1.12) ⋯→𝑥R→𝑦R→𝑥R→𝑦R→𝜀M⟶0.\cdots\xrightarrow{\,x\,}R\xrightarrow{\,y\,}R\xrightarrow{\,x\,}R\xrightarrow{\,y\,}R\xrightarrow{\,\varepsilon\,}M\longrightarrow 0.

We verify exactness at every term.

At F0F_{0}, the kernel of ε\varepsilon is the ideal (y)=y​R(y)=yR, while the image of d1d_{1} is also y​RyR. Hence the complex is exact at F0F_{0}. Now let i≥1i\geq 1. If ii is odd, then did_{i} is multiplication by yy, so

kerdi=(0:Ry)=xR\ker d_{i}=(0:_{R}y)=xR

by (1.11). Since i+1i+1 is even, di+1d_{i+1} is multiplication by xx, and therefore

This resolution is minimal because every differential is represented by the 1×11\times 1 matrix (x)(x) or (y)(y), and both entries belong to the maximal ideal 𝔪\mathfrak{m}.

Step 5: tensoring with NN and computing Tor.

By definition, if F∙→MF_{\bullet}\to M is a free resolution, then

ToriR⁡(M,N)=Hi​(F∙⊗RN).\operatorname{Tor}_{i}^{R}(M,N)=H_{i}(F_{\bullet}\otimes_{R}N).

We therefore tensor the free resolution (1.12) with NN. For every ii, the natural map

R⊗RN⟶N,r⊗n⟼r​n,R\otimes_{R}N\longrightarrow N,\qquad r\otimes n\longmapsto rn,

is an isomorphism. Under this identification, tensoring a map given by multiplication by xx or by yy produces the corresponding multiplication map on NN. But in NN the elements xx and yy have the same image uu. Hence the complex F∙⊗RNF_{\bullet}\otimes_{R}N is

(1.13) ⋯→𝑢N→𝑢N→𝑢N.\cdots\xrightarrow{\,u\,}N\xrightarrow{\,u\,}N\xrightarrow{\,u\,}N.

We calculate the kernel and image of multiplication by uu directly. Every element of N≅K⁡[u]/(u2)N\cong K[u]/(u^{2}) has a unique expression a+b​ua+bu with a,b∈Ka,b\in K, and

u⁡(a+b​u)=a​u+b​u2=a​u.u(a+bu)=au+bu^{2}=au.

Therefore

u(a+bu)=0⟺a=0⟺a+bu∈Ku.u(a+bu)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a+bu\in Ku.

Thus

ker(u:N→N)=Ku.\ker(u:N\to N)=Ku.

Also, the displayed formula shows that every image is a scalar multiple of uu, and every scalar multiple of uu occurs as u⁡(a)u(a). Hence

im(u:N→N)=Ku.\operatorname{im}(u:N\to N)=Ku.

The kernel of each differential in (1.13) is therefore equal to the image of the next differential. The complex is exact in every positive homological degree, and consequently

(1.14) ToriR⁡(M,N)=0for every ​i≥1.\operatorname{Tor}_{i}^{R}(M,N)=0\qquad\text{for every }i\geq 1.

We have proved that RR is a commutative Artinian local ring with unique maximal ideal 𝔪=(x,y)\mathfrak{m}=(x,y); that MM and NN are nonzero finitely generated modules satisfying 𝔪2​M=𝔪2​N=0\mathfrak{m}^{2}M=\mathfrak{m}^{2}N=0; and that all positive Tor groups ToriR⁡(M,N)\operatorname{Tor}_{i}^{R}(M,N) vanish. At the same time, (1.7) gives

𝔪3=K​y3≠0.\mathfrak{m}^{3}=Ky^{3}\neq 0.

∎

2. A negative answer to a question of Avramov, Buchweitz and Şega

In this section we prove the following, which gives a negative answer to the question of Avramov, Buchweitz and Şega as explained in the introduction.

There exists a finite-dimensional commutative local non-Gorenstein ℚ\mathbb{Q}-algebra RR such that ExtR1⁡(D⁡(R),R)=0\operatorname{Ext}_{R}^{1}(D(R),R)=0.

The proof is a computer verification in Magma. We first explain the individual steps. Since BasicAlgebra starts from a free associative algebra, the script adds all 153 commutator relations before adjoining the 144 quadratic relations displayed above. It then computes the successive radicals of the regular module. Their dimensions are

48, 47, 29, 2, 0,48,\ 47,\ 29,\ 2,\ 0,

so the radical layers have dimensions (1,18,27,2)(1,18,27,2). In particular, the top of the regular module is one-dimensional, and hence RR is local. The socle of RRR_{R} has dimension two. Since a commutative Artinian local algebra is Gorenstein precisely when its socle is one-dimensional, this proves that RR is not Gorenstein.

Because RR is local, its unique indecomposable injective module is isomorphic to D⁡(R)D(R). The command InjectiveModule(R,1) constructs this module. If

0⟶Ω⟶P0⟶D⁡(R)⟶00\longrightarrow\Omega\longrightarrow P_{0}\longrightarrow D(R)\longrightarrow 0

is its projective cover sequence, then applying HomR⁡(−,R)\operatorname{Hom}_{R}(-,R) gives

dimKExtR1⁡(D⁡(R),R)=dimKHomR⁡(Ω,R)−dimKHomR⁡(P0,R)+dimKHomR⁡(D⁡(R),R).\dim_{K}\operatorname{Ext}_{R}^{1}(D(R),R)=\dim_{K}\operatorname{Hom}_{R}(\Omega,R)-\dim_{K}\operatorname{Hom}_{R}(P_{0},R)+\dim_{K}\operatorname{Hom}_{R}(D(R),R).

The final part of the script computes these three Hom spaces and evaluates this alternating sum.

Thus RR has all the properties claimed in the theorem. We also verified the computation independently using the GAP package QPA [QPA]. For this algebra one has ExtR2⁡(D⁡(R),R)≠0\operatorname{Ext}_{R}^{2}(D(R),R)\neq 0, so the example is not a counterexample to the first Tachikawa conjecture itself.

3. A negative answer to a question of Dao

The main theorem of this section is as follows:

Theorem 3.1.

Let K=𝔽2K=\mathbb{F}_{2}. There is a finite-dimensional commutative local self-injective KK-algebra RR admitting an indecomposable non-projective RR-module MM such that

ExtR1⁡(M,M)=0=ExtR2⁡(M,M).\operatorname{Ext}_{R}^{1}(M,M)=0=\operatorname{Ext}_{R}^{2}(M,M).

Let

(3.1) I=(xi​xj+x1​ℓi,j∣2≤i≤j≤14)andR=S/I.I=\bigl(x_{i}x_{j}+x_{1}\ell_{i,j}\mid 2\leq i\leq j\leq 14\bigr)\qquad\text{and}\qquad R=S/I.

Here the plus sign is the same as a minus sign because K=𝔽2K=\mathbb{F}_{2}. Thus every quadratic monomial involving only x2,…,x14x_{2},\ldots,x_{14} is expressed as a linear combination of

x12,x1​x2,…,x1​x14.x_{1}^{2},x_{1}x_{2},\ldots,x_{1}x_{14}.

The computation below gives

dimKR=30and(dimK(R/𝔪),dimK(𝔪/𝔪2),dimK(𝔪2/𝔪3),dimK𝔪3)=(1,14,14,1),\dim_{K}R=30\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bigl(\dim_{K}(R/\mathfrak{m}),\dim_{K}(\mathfrak{m}/\mathfrak{m}^{2}),\dim_{K}(\mathfrak{m}^{2}/\mathfrak{m}^{3}),\dim_{K}\mathfrak{m}^{3}\bigr)=(1,14,14,1),

where 𝔪=(x1,…,x14)​R\mathfrak{m}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{14})R. In particular, RR is local with radical-series dimensions

30, 29, 15, 1, 0.30,\ 29,\ 15,\ 1,\ 0.

Moreover, the socle of RRR_{R} is one-dimensional. Hence the commutative Artinian local algebra RR is Gorenstein and therefore self-injective.

We now give the module by an explicit minimal projective presentation. Let f1,f2f_{1},f_{2} be the standard basis of R2R^{2}, and let e1,e2,e3e_{1},e_{2},e_{3} be the standard basis of R3R^{3}. Define

d1:R3⟶R2,d1​(ej)=aj​f1+bj​f2,d_{1}:R^{3}\longrightarrow R^{2},\qquad d_{1}(e_{j})=a_{j}f_{1}+b_{j}f_{2},

where

a1\displaystyle a_{1} =x1+x3+x5,\displaystyle=x_{1}+x_{3}+x_{5}, b1\displaystyle b_{1} =x1+x3+x5+x8+x11+x12,\displaystyle=x_{1}+x_{3}+x_{5}+x_{8}+x_{11}+x_{12},
a2\displaystyle a_{2} =x2+x4+x5+x6+x7+x9+x10+x12,\displaystyle=x_{2}+x_{4}+x_{5}+x_{6}+x_{7}+x_{9}+x_{10}+x_{12}, b2\displaystyle b_{2} =x4+x5+x7+x12,\displaystyle=x_{4}+x_{5}+x_{7}+x_{12},
a3\displaystyle a_{3} =x2+x3+x6+x8+x11+x14,\displaystyle=x_{2}+x_{3}+x_{6}+x_{8}+x_{11}+x_{14}, b3\displaystyle b_{3} =x2+x6+x8+x10+x12+x13+x14.\displaystyle=x_{2}+x_{6}+x_{8}+x_{10}+x_{12}+x_{13}+x_{14}.

Equivalently, d1d_{1} is represented by the matrix

(3.2) (a1a2a3b1b2b3).\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}a_{1}&a_{2}&a_{3}\\ b_{1}&b_{2}&b_{3}\end{array}\right).

Set

(3.3) M=coker⁡(d1),R3→d1R2⟶M⟶0.M=\operatorname{coker}(d_{1}),\qquad R^{3}\xrightarrow{\ d_{1}\ }R^{2}\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow 0.

All entries of the presentation matrix lie in 𝔪\mathfrak{m}, so the presentation is minimal. Its image has dimension 2929, and consequently dimKM=60−29=31\dim_{K}M=60-29=31. The radical-series dimensions of MM are

31, 29, 4, 0,31,\ 29,\ 4,\ 0,

so the radical layers have dimensions (2,25,4)(2,25,4). Magma’s decomposition routine returns a single summand, so MM is indecomposable. The module is not projective: over the local algebra RR, every finitely generated projective module is free, whereas 3030 does not divide 3131.

For completeness, we explain the numerical Ext calculation used in the script. Put Ω1=ΩR​(M)\Omega_{1}=\Omega_{R}(M). The map R2→MR^{2}\to M in (3.3) is a projective cover, dimKΩ1=29\dim_{K}\Omega_{1}=29, and R3→Ω1R^{3}\to\Omega_{1} is a projective cover with kernel Ω2=ΩR2​(M)\Omega_{2}=\Omega_{R}^{2}(M) of dimension 6161. Applying HomR⁡(−,M)\operatorname{Hom}_{R}(-,M) to the first two short exact sequences in the minimal projective resolution gives

dimKExtR1⁡(M,M)\displaystyle\dim_{K}\operatorname{Ext}_{R}^{1}(M,M) =dimKHomR⁡(Ω1,M)−dimKHomR⁡(R2,M)+dimKEndR⁡(M),\displaystyle=\dim_{K}\operatorname{Hom}_{R}(\Omega_{1},M)-\dim_{K}\operatorname{Hom}_{R}(R^{2},M)+\dim_{K}\operatorname{End}_{R}(M),
dimKExtR2⁡(M,M)\displaystyle\dim_{K}\operatorname{Ext}_{R}^{2}(M,M) =dimKHomR⁡(Ω2,M)−dimKHomR⁡(R3,M)+dimKHomR⁡(Ω1,M).\displaystyle=\dim_{K}\operatorname{Hom}_{R}(\Omega_{2},M)-\dim_{K}\operatorname{Hom}_{R}(R^{3},M)+\dim_{K}\operatorname{Hom}_{R}(\Omega_{1},M).

The computed dimensions are

dimKEndR⁡(M)=47,dimKHomR⁡(Ω1,M)=15,dimKHomR⁡(Ω2,M)=78.\dim_{K}\operatorname{End}_{R}(M)=47,\qquad\dim_{K}\operatorname{Hom}_{R}(\Omega_{1},M)=15,\qquad\dim_{K}\operatorname{Hom}_{R}(\Omega_{2},M)=78.

Since dimKHomR⁡(R2,M)=62\dim_{K}\operatorname{Hom}_{R}(R^{2},M)=62 and dimKHomR⁡(R3,M)=93\dim_{K}\operatorname{Hom}_{R}(R^{3},M)=93, this yields

dimKExtR1⁡(M,M)=15−62+47=0,dimKExtR2⁡(M,M)=78−93+15=0.\dim_{K}\operatorname{Ext}_{R}^{1}(M,M)=15-62+47=0,\qquad\dim_{K}\operatorname{Ext}_{R}^{2}(M,M)=78-93+15=0.

4. Two conjectures

We record two conjectures that would follow from Yamagata’s conjecture and may be of particular interest to commutative algebraists, where Yamagata’s conjecture might not be well known so far. Recall that the dominant dimension measures the length of the initial projective part of the minimal injective resolution of the regular module. Yamagata’s conjecture predicts that, for finite-dimensional, not necessarily commutative, non-self-injective algebras, the dominant dimension is bounded by a function depending only on the number of simple modules. Via the standard Morita–Tachikawa construction, the relevant algebras where the dominant dimension is of interest are EndR⁡(M)\operatorname{End}_{R}(M) for a generator-cogenerator MM of mod⁡R\operatorname{mod}R and the dominant dimensions of such endomorphism rings are determined by the corresponding initial Ext-vanishing ranges. Thus Yamagata’s conjecture would imply uniform finite-vanishing versions of both Tachikawa conjectures in the commutative local case. For more precise formulations of Yamagata’s conjecture, partial results and related applications, see [Y, M, CFKKY]. Yamagata’s conjecture would imply the next two conjectures in this section that we want to popularize here.

Conjecture.

There exists an integer n≥1n\geq 1 such that, for every commutative local finite-dimensional algebra RR, the vanishing

ExtRi⁡(D⁡(R),R)=0for ​i=1,…,n\operatorname{Ext}_{R}^{i}(D(R),R)=0\qquad\text{for }i=1,\ldots,n

implies that RR is Gorenstein.

The example in Section 2 shows that n=1n=1 is impossible. It remains open whether n=2n=2 suffices. This is a uniform finite-vanishing strengthening of the first Tachikawa conjecture.

The analogous strengthening of the second Tachikawa conjecture is the following.

Conjecture.

There exists an integer n≥1n\geq 1 such that, for every commutative local finite-dimensional Gorenstein algebra RR and every indecomposable RR-module MM, the vanishing

ExtRi⁡(M,M)=0for ​i=1,…,n\operatorname{Ext}_{R}^{i}(M,M)=0\qquad\text{for }i=1,\ldots,n

implies that MM is projective.

The example in Section 3 shows that n≤2n\leq 2 is impossible. It remains open whether n=3n=3 suffices.

Statement on the use of AI

Generative AI tools, namely ChatGPT, were used during the exploratory and preparatory stages of this work. The mathematical strategy and proofs were conceived and directed by the authors. ChatGPT assisted with selected aspects of the technical development, including the formulation of auxiliary results and the elaboration of technical details, as well as with literature searches, consistency checks, and LaTeX preparation. All AI-generated suggestions were independently reviewed and verified by the authors, who assume full responsibility for the mathematical arguments, results, and final content of the paper.
